about: ST109 is an Autumn Term half unit, compulsory on the BSc Economics and BSc Econometrics and Mathematical Economics, that gives a rigorous introduction to probability and distribution theory assuming no prior statistics (A-level Mathematics is required). The 2026/27 course guide lists five areas: data visualisation and descriptive statistics, probability theory, random variables, common distributions of random variables, and multivariate random variables; this pack splits probability and the named distributions into two parts each for revision. Teaching is 20 hours of lectures, 15 hours of classes and 11 hours of workshops in Autumn Term, with weekly exercises for feedback. Assessment is a single 2-hour exam (plus 10 minutes' reading time) in the January exam period worth 100%; the recommended supplementary text is Larsen and Marx, Introduction to Mathematical Statistics and Its Applications.
topics: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem
Random variables: distributions, expectation and variance

notes.h: Describing data: graphs and summary statistics
notes.body:
ST109 begins with how to summarise a data set before any probability is introduced. Exam questions typically ask you to compute summaries by hand and to say which summary or graph suits the data.

Types of variable
- Categorical (nominal, such as degree programme; or ordinal, such as satisfaction ratings) versus numerical (discrete counts or continuous measurements).
- The type of variable decides which graphs and summaries make sense.

Graphs
- Bar charts for categorical data; histograms for continuous data (area of each bar proportional to frequency, so unequal class widths need frequency density).
- Boxplots show the median, the quartiles (box), whiskers and outliers; good for comparing groups.
- Scatter plots show the relationship between two numerical variables.
- Read the shape: centre, spread, skewness, outliers and multiple peaks.

Measures of location
- Sample mean x̄ = (1/n) Σ xi.
- Median: the middle ordered value (average of the two middle values when n is even).
- Mode: the most frequent value.
- The median is robust to outliers; the mean is not.

Measures of spread
- Range = maximum − minimum.
- Sample variance s² = Σ(xi − x̄)² / (n − 1). Shortcut: s² = (Σxi² − n x̄²) / (n − 1).
- Sample standard deviation s = √s² (same units as the data).
- Interquartile range IQR = Q3 − Q1, robust to outliers. Conventions for computing quartiles differ, so follow the one in your lecture notes.

Worked example
Data: 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 10 (n = 6).
- Mean = 30/6 = 5. Median = (3 + 5)/2 = 4. Mode = 3. Range = 8.
- Deviations from the mean: −3, −2, −2, 0, 2, 5; squared: 9, 4, 4, 0, 4, 25; sum 46.
- s² = 46/5 = 9.2 and s ≈ 3.03.
- Shortcut check: Σx² = 196 and n x̄² = 150, so s² = (196 − 150)/5 = 9.2.
- Mean > median, which points to positive (right) skew: the value 10 pulls the mean up.

Skewness
- Positive (right) skew: a long right tail, typically mean > median (incomes, house prices).
- Negative (left) skew: a long left tail, typically mean < median.
- Symmetric: mean and median roughly equal.

Effects of linear transformations
If yi = a + bxi, then ȳ = a + b x̄ and sy = |b| sx. Adding a constant shifts location but not spread; multiplying rescales both.

Why divide by n − 1?
Deviations are measured from x̄ rather than the unknown population mean, and they sum to zero, so only n − 1 are free. Dividing by n − 1 makes s² an unbiased estimator of the population variance, a result you will meet formally later.

Exam tips: show the table of deviations when computing s², state the divisor you used, and when asked to compare summaries, explain robustness to outliers and skewness.

notes.h: Probability: sample spaces, axioms and counting
notes.body:
Probability gives a precise language for uncertainty. ST109 develops it from axioms, so you are expected to prove simple results as well as compute probabilities.

Basic set-up
- Experiment: a process with an uncertain outcome. Sample space S: the set of all possible outcomes.
- Event: a subset of S. Use set operations: union A ∪ B (A or B), intersection A ∩ B (A and B), complement Aᶜ (not A).
- Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events: A ∩ B = ∅.
- De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ and (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ.

Axioms (Kolmogorov)
1. P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A.
2. P(S) = 1.
3. If A1, A2, … are pairwise mutually exclusive, P(A1 ∪ A2 ∪ …) = P(A1) + P(A2) + ….

Results proved from the axioms
- P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A), since A and Aᶜ are disjoint with union S.
- P(∅) = 0.
- If A ⊆ B then P(A) ≤ P(B).
- Addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Proof: write A ∪ B as the disjoint union of A and B ∩ Aᶜ, and B as the disjoint union of A ∩ B and B ∩ Aᶜ.
- Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2 gives P(A ∪ B) = 0.7, and P(exactly one) = P(A ∪ B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.5.

Equally likely outcomes
If S has N equally likely outcomes and A contains n of them, P(A) = n/N. Counting is then the whole problem.

Counting rules
- Multiplication principle: k stages with n1, n2, …, nk options give n1 × n2 × … × nk outcomes.
- Ordered selections without replacement (permutations): nPr = n!/(n − r)!.
- Unordered selections without replacement (combinations): nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!).
- Ordered with replacement: n^r.
- Example: the number of 5-card hands from 52 cards is 52C5 = 2,598,960.
- Example: a committee of 3 is chosen at random from 4 women and 6 men. P(exactly 2 women) = (4C2 × 6C1)/10C3 = (6 × 6)/120 = 0.3.
- Keep numerator and denominator consistent: both ordered or both unordered.

Complement trick
For "at least one" problems, compute 1 − P(none). For example, the probability that at least two of k people share a birthday is 1 minus the probability that all k birthdays differ (assuming 365 equally likely days).

Classical, frequency and subjective views
Equally likely outcomes give classical probabilities; long-run relative frequencies give frequentist probabilities; subjective probabilities express degrees of belief. All satisfy the same axioms.

Exam tips: draw a Venn diagram, define events with letters before calculating, and when proving results, cite which axiom you use at each step.

notes.h: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem
notes.body:
Conditioning is how probabilities are updated when information arrives. It is the most tested idea in the probability part of ST109.

Conditional probability
- For P(B) > 0, P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).
- Multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)P(B) = P(B | A)P(A).
- Chain rule: P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A) P(B | A) P(C | A ∩ B).
- For fixed B, P(· | B) satisfies all the axioms, so results such as P(Aᶜ | B) = 1 − P(A | B) carry over.

Independence
- A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Equivalently (when P(B) > 0), P(A | B) = P(A).
- If A and B are independent, so are A and Bᶜ, Aᶜ and B, and Aᶜ and Bᶜ.
- Mutual independence of three events needs all pairwise conditions and P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A)P(B)P(C). Pairwise independence alone is not enough.
- Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. If P(A) > 0, P(B) > 0 and A ∩ B = ∅, then P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B), so disjoint events with positive probability are always dependent: knowing one happened tells you the other did not.

Law of total probability
If B1, …, Bk partition S (mutually exclusive, union S, each with positive probability), then
P(A) = Σ P(A | Bi) P(Bi).

Bayes' theorem
If B1, …, Bk partition S with each P(Bi) > 0, and P(A) > 0, then
P(Bj | A) = P(A | Bj) P(Bj) / Σ P(A | Bi) P(Bi).
- The denominator is P(A), from the law of total probability.
- P(Bj) is the prior; P(Bj | A) is the posterior.

Worked example: medical testing
A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it in 95% of those who have it (sensitivity), and gives a positive result for 10% of those who do not (false positive rate).
- P(D ∩ +) = 0.01 × 0.95 = 0.0095.
- P(Dᶜ ∩ +) = 0.99 × 0.10 = 0.099.
- P(+) = 0.0095 + 0.099 = 0.1085.
- P(D | +) = 0.0095/0.1085 ≈ 0.088.
Fewer than 1 in 11 people who test positive have the disease. Because the disease is rare, false positives from the large healthy group outnumber true positives. Confusing P(+ | D) = 0.95 with P(D | +) is the classic error (sometimes called the prosecutor's fallacy in legal settings).

Worked example: factories
Factory A makes 60% of items with a 2% defect rate; factory B makes 40% with a 5% defect rate.
- P(defective) = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.032.
- P(A | defective) = 0.012/0.032 = 0.375.

Tree diagrams
Branches carry conditional probabilities; multiply along a path for the joint probability and add across paths for a total probability. They make Bayes problems hard to get wrong.

Exam tips: write the conditional you want in symbols first, define the partition, and show P(A) from total probability before dividing.

notes.h: Random variables: distributions, expectation and variance
notes.body:
A random variable is a function that assigns a number to each outcome in the sample space. ST109 treats discrete and continuous random variables in parallel, so learn the two sets of formulae side by side.

Discrete random variables
- Probability mass function (pmf): p(x) = P(X = x), with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ p(x) = 1.
- Cumulative distribution function (cdf): F(x) = P(X ≤ x), a non-decreasing step function from 0 to 1.

Continuous random variables
- Probability density function (pdf) f(x) ≥ 0 with ∫ f(x) dx = 1 over the whole real line.
- P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx; P(X = x) = 0 for any single x, so ≤ and < give the same probabilities.
- cdf F(x) = ∫ from −∞ to x of f(t) dt, and f(x) = F′(x) where the derivative exists.
- A density can exceed 1; only areas are probabilities.

Expectation
- Discrete: E(X) = Σ x p(x). Continuous: E(X) = ∫ x f(x) dx.
- For a function g: E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) p(x) or ∫ g(x) f(x) dx.
- Linearity: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b.
- In general E[g(X)] ≠ g(E[X]); for example E(X²) ≠ (E X)² unless X is constant.

Variance
- Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E(X²) − (E X)², with μ = E(X).
- Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X): adding a constant does not change spread, and the multiplier is squared.
- Standard deviation = √Var(X).

Worked example (discrete)
P(X = 0) = 0.2, P(X = 1) = 0.5, P(X = 2) = 0.3.
- E(X) = 0 + 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1.
- E(X²) = 0 + 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7.
- Var(X) = 1.7 − 1.21 = 0.49, so the SD is 0.7.

Worked example (continuous)
f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 (0 otherwise).
- Check: ∫ 2x dx from 0 to 1 = 1.
- F(x) = x² on [0, 1].
- E(X) = ∫ 2x² dx = 2/3; E(X²) = ∫ 2x³ dx = 1/2; Var(X) = 1/2 − 4/9 = 1/18.
- Median m solves F(m) = 1/2: m = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. Here the median exceeds the mean (0.667), as expected for a left-skewed density.

Other summaries
- Quantiles: the p-quantile solves F(x) = p.
- Mode: the value maximising p(x) or f(x).

Moment generating functions
The 2026/27 ST109 course guide does not list moment generating functions among its topics, so check your lecture notes before revising them. If you do meet them: MX(t) = E(e^(tX)); if it is finite for all t in an open interval around 0, it determines the distribution uniquely, and its derivatives at t = 0 give the moments: M′(0) = E(X) and M″(0) = E(X²).

Transformations
If Y = g(X) with g strictly increasing, FY(y) = P(X ≤ g⁻¹(y)) = FX(g⁻¹(y)). Working through the cdf is the safest method; differentiate to get the pdf.

Exam tips: always check that a proposed pmf or pdf is valid (non-negative and sums or integrates to 1) before using it, and show E(X²) explicitly when computing variances.

A small set of named distributions covers most discrete modelling in ST109. For each, know the setting, the pmf, the mean and variance, and when it approximates another.

Bernoulli(p)
- One trial with success probability p: P(X = 1) = p, P(X = 0) = 1 − p.
- E(X) = p, Var(X) = p(1 − p).

Binomial(n, p)
- Number of successes in n independent trials, each with the same success probability p.
- P(X = x) = nCx p^x (1 − p)^(n − x), for x = 0, 1, …, n.
- E(X) = np, Var(X) = np(1 − p). These follow from writing X as a sum of n independent Bernoulli variables.
- Example: n = 10, p = 0.3. P(X = 2) = 45 × 0.3² × 0.7⁸ ≈ 0.2335 and P(X ≤ 2) ≈ 0.3828.
- Check the conditions: fixed n, independence, constant p, two outcomes. Sampling without replacement from a small population breaks independence.

Geometric(p)
- Number of trials up to and including the first success: P(X = x) = (1 − p)^(x − 1) p, for x = 1, 2, ….
- E(X) = 1/p, Var(X) = (1 − p)/p².
- Example: p = 0.2 gives P(X = 3) = 0.8² × 0.2 = 0.128 and E(X) = 5.
- It is memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).
- Some books count failures before the first success instead, which shifts the mean to (1 − p)/p, so check the definition used.

Poisson(λ)
- Counts of events occurring randomly and independently at a constant average rate in a fixed interval (calls per minute, typos per page).
- P(X = x) = e^(−λ) λ^x / x!, for x = 0, 1, 2, ….
- E(X) = Var(X) = λ.
- Example: λ = 2 per minute. P(X = 0) = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135. P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(0) − P(1) = 1 − 3e^(−2) ≈ 0.594.
- Rate scaling: if events occur at 2 per minute, the count in 3 minutes is Poisson(6).
- Approximation: Binomial(n, p) ≈ Poisson(np) when n is large and p small. For n = 100, p = 0.02: exact P(X = 0) ≈ 0.1326 versus Poisson e^(−2) ≈ 0.1353.

Hypergeometric
- Number of successes in a sample of size n drawn without replacement from N items of which K are successes.
- P(X = x) = (KCx × (N − K)C(n − x)) / NCn.
- Mean nK/N, the same as the binomial with p = K/N, but a smaller variance (when n > 1) because of the finite population.
- The committee example (exactly 2 women out of 3 chosen from 4 women and 6 men) is hypergeometric: 0.3.

Discrete uniform
Each of k values equally likely: for values 1, …, k, E(X) = (k + 1)/2.

Choosing a model
Ask: is there a fixed number of trials (binomial)? Waiting for a first success (geometric)? Counting events in continuous time or space (Poisson)? Sampling without replacement (hypergeometric)?

Exam tips: name the distribution and its parameters before calculating, state the assumptions that justify it, and use complements for "at least" probabilities.

notes.h: Common continuous distributions: uniform, exponential and normal
notes.body:
Three continuous distributions do most of the work in ST109 and in later statistics and econometrics.

Continuous uniform U(a, b)
- f(x) = 1/(b − a) for a ≤ x ≤ b.
- F(x) = (x − a)/(b − a) on [a, b].
- E(X) = (a + b)/2, Var(X) = (b − a)²/12.
- Example: U(2, 8) has mean 5 and variance 36/12 = 3.

Exponential(λ)
- Waiting time until the next event in a Poisson process with rate λ.
- f(x) = λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0; F(x) = 1 − e^(−λx); P(X > x) = e^(−λx).
- E(X) = 1/λ, Var(X) = 1/λ². Watch the parametrisation: some books use the mean θ = 1/λ instead.
- Memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). Proof: P(X > s + t)/P(X > s) = e^(−λ(s+t))/e^(−λs) = e^(−λt).
- Example: lifetime with mean 2 years (λ = 0.5). Given it has lasted 2 years, the probability it lasts at least 2 more is e^(−1) ≈ 0.368, the same as for a new item.
- Link to Poisson: the waiting time exceeds t exactly when there are no events in [0, t], so P(T > t) = e^(−λt).

Normal N(μ, σ²)
- f(x) = (1/(σ√(2π))) exp(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)), symmetric and bell-shaped about μ.
- E(X) = μ, Var(X) = σ². Note: the second parameter is the variance.
- Standardisation: Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1). Use tables of Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z), with Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).
- Example: X ~ N(50, 16), so σ = 4. P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668. P(46 < X < 58) = Φ(2) − Φ(−1) ≈ 0.8186.
- Useful values: P(|Z| < 1.96) ≈ 0.95; P(|Z| < 1) ≈ 0.683; P(|Z| < 2) ≈ 0.954.
- Linear functions: if X ~ N(μ, σ²) then aX + b ~ N(aμ + b, a²σ²).
- Sums: independent normals add to a normal, with means adding and variances adding.

Normal approximation to the binomial
- For large n with p not too close to 0 or 1 (a common rule: np and n(1 − p) both above about 5), Binomial(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)).
- Use a continuity correction: P(X ≤ k) ≈ Φ((k + 0.5 − np)/√(np(1 − p))).
- Example: X ~ Bin(100, 0.5). P(X ≤ 55) ≈ Φ(5.5/5) = Φ(1.1) ≈ 0.864; the exact value is also about 0.864. Without the correction you would get Φ(1) ≈ 0.841.

Finding quantiles
To find x with P(X ≤ x) = p, find z with Φ(z) = p and use x = μ + zσ. For example, the top 5% of N(50, 16) starts at 50 + 1.645 × 4 ≈ 56.6.

Exam tips: convert variance to standard deviation before standardising, sketch the normal curve and shade the area you need, and state the continuity correction explicitly.

notes.h: Multivariate random variables: joint distributions, covariance and sums
notes.body:
The final ST109 topic handles two or more random variables at once. This is the foundation for regression in EC1C1 and later statistics courses.

Joint and marginal distributions
- Discrete: joint pmf p(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y), with Σ Σ p(x, y) = 1.
- Marginals: pX(x) = Σ over y of p(x, y), and similarly for Y (row and column totals of the table).
- Continuous: joint pdf f(x, y), with probabilities given by double integrals and marginals by integrating out the other variable.

Conditional distributions
- p(y | x) = p(x, y)/pX(x) for pX(x) > 0.
- Conditional expectation E(Y | X = x) = Σ y p(y | x).
- Law of iterated expectations: E(Y) = E[E(Y | X)].

Independence
- X and Y are independent if p(x, y) = pX(x) pY(y) for all x and y (or f(x, y) = fX(x) fY(y)).
- One cell that fails the product rule is enough to show dependence.

Covariance and correlation
- Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μX)(Y − μY)] = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y).
- Corr(X, Y) = Cov(X, Y)/(σX σY), always between −1 and 1, equal to ±1 only for an exact linear relationship.
- Correlation measures linear association only and is unit-free.
- Independence implies zero covariance, but not conversely. Example: X equally likely to be −1, 0 or 1 and Y = X². Then E(X) = 0 and E(XY) = E(X³) = 0, so Cov = 0, yet Y is a function of X.

Worked example
Joint pmf of X and Y (both 0 or 1): p(0,0) = 0.3, p(0,1) = 0.2, p(1,0) = 0.1, p(1,1) = 0.4.
- Marginals: P(X = 1) = 0.5, P(Y = 1) = 0.6, so E(X) = 0.5 and E(Y) = 0.6.
- E(XY) = P(X = 1, Y = 1) = 0.4, so Cov = 0.4 − 0.3 = 0.1.
- Var(X) = 0.25 and Var(Y) = 0.24, so Corr = 0.1/√0.06 ≈ 0.41.
- Not independent: p(1,1) = 0.4 but 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.3.
- P(Y = 1 | X = 1) = 0.8 and P(Y = 1 | X = 0) = 0.4.

Sums and linear combinations
- E(aX + bY) = aE(X) + bE(Y), always.
- Var(aX + bY) = a²Var(X) + b²Var(Y) + 2ab Cov(X, Y).
- In the example, Var(X + Y) = 0.25 + 0.24 + 0.2 = 0.69.
- For independent X1, …, Xn: Var(ΣXi) = ΣVar(Xi).
- Sample mean of n independent variables with mean μ and variance σ²: E(X̄) = μ and Var(X̄) = σ²/n. This is the bridge to statistical inference.
- Covariance rules: Cov(aX, bY) = ab Cov(X, Y); Cov(X, X) = Var(X); Cov(X, Y + Z) = Cov(X, Y) + Cov(X, Z).

Useful closure results
- Sum of independent Poisson(λ1) and Poisson(λ2) is Poisson(λ1 + λ2).
- Sum of independent binomials with the same p is binomial.
- Sum of independent normals is normal.

Exam tips: lay out the joint table with row and column totals, compute E(XY) cell by cell, and remember that the covariance term carries the factor 2ab, with its sign.

cards.b: E(X̄) = μ and Var(X̄) = σ²/n.

questions.q: What is the sample variance (divisor n − 1) of the data 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 10?
questions.why: The mean is 5 and the squared deviations sum to 46, so s² = 46/5 = 9.2. The value 7.67 divides by n = 6 instead of n − 1. The value 3.03 is the standard deviation, the square root of the variance. The value 14.2 comes from a broken shortcut, Σx²/(n − 1) − x̄² = 196/5 − 25; the correct shortcut subtracts n x̄² before dividing: (196 − 150)/5 = 9.2.

questions.q: Household incomes have a long right tail. What would you expect of their distribution?
options: Positively skewed, with the mean equal to the median
Positively skewed, with the mean above the median
Negatively skewed, with the mean above the median
Positively skewed, with the median above the mean
questions.why: A long right tail is positive (right) skew, and the few very large values pull the mean above the median. Calling it negatively skewed confuses the naming: skew is named after the side of the long tail. Having the median above the mean is the pattern for a long left tail. Equal mean and median is typical of a symmetric distribution, not a skewed one.

questions.q: A researcher wants to summarise the wealth of 500 households, which includes a few billionaires. Which measures of location and spread should she report, and which graph would you recommend? Justify your choices.
markScheme: Recommends the median as the measure of location because it is robust to extreme values
Recommends the IQR (or quartiles) for spread, since variance and SD are inflated by outliers
Notes the mean exceeds the median because of positive skew, and both may be reported to show this
Recommends a boxplot or histogram (possibly on a log scale) and explains what it shows
questions.modelAnswer: Wealth data are strongly positively skewed, and a few billionaires would drag the mean far above the typical household's wealth. The median is robust to such extreme values, so it is the better measure of location; reporting the mean alongside it is informative because the gap between them shows the degree of skew. For spread, the variance and standard deviation depend on squared deviations and would be dominated by the outliers, so the interquartile range (Q3 − Q1) is more representative of the bulk of households. A boxplot shows the median, quartiles and outliers at a glance, while a histogram (perhaps of log wealth, which reduces the skew) shows the overall shape.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.why: Addition rule: 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. The value 0.9 adds P(A) and P(B) as though the events were mutually exclusive, counting the overlap twice. The value 0.2 is the intersection, not the union. The value 0.5 is the probability that exactly one of the events occurs, 0.7 − 0.2, which leaves out the outcomes where both occur.

questions.q: A committee of 3 is chosen at random from 4 women and 6 men. What is the probability that it contains exactly 2 women?
questions.why: There are 10C3 = 120 equally likely committees, of which 4C2 × 6C1 = 36 have exactly two women, so the probability is 36/120 = 0.3. The value 0.288 is the binomial 3 × 0.4² × 0.6, which treats the choices as made with replacement. The value 0.05 divides the unordered count 36 by the ordered count 10 × 9 × 8 = 720, mixing ordered and unordered counting. The value 0.333 is the probability of at least two women, (36 + 4)/120, which adds the all-women committees.

questions.q: State Kolmogorov's axioms of probability. Using them, prove that P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) and that P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
markScheme: States the three axioms correctly (non-negativity, P(S) = 1, countable additivity for disjoint events)
Complement: A and Aᶜ are disjoint with union S, so P(A) + P(Aᶜ) = 1
Writes A ∪ B = A ∪ (B ∩ Aᶜ) as a disjoint union
Writes B = (A ∩ B) ∪ (B ∩ Aᶜ) as a disjoint union and eliminates P(B ∩ Aᶜ)
Cites the axiom used at each step
questions.modelAnswer: Axioms: (1) P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A; (2) P(S) = 1; (3) if A1, A2, … are pairwise disjoint, P(∪Ai) = ΣP(Ai). Complement: A and Aᶜ are disjoint and A ∪ Aᶜ = S. By axiom 3, P(A) + P(Aᶜ) = P(S), which equals 1 by axiom 2, so P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A). Addition rule: A ∪ B is the disjoint union of A and B ∩ Aᶜ, so by axiom 3, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B ∩ Aᶜ). Also B is the disjoint union of A ∩ B and B ∩ Aᶜ, so P(B) = P(A ∩ B) + P(B ∩ Aᶜ), giving P(B ∩ Aᶜ) = P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Substituting, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

questions.q: A disease affects 1% of people. A test is positive for 95% of those with the disease and for 10% of those without it. What is the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease?
questions.why: Bayes: P(D | +) = (0.01 × 0.95)/(0.01 × 0.95 + 0.99 × 0.10) = 0.0095/0.1085 ≈ 0.088. The value 0.95 is P(+ | D), the reverse conditional. The value 0.0095 is the joint probability P(D ∩ +), which still needs dividing by P(+) = 0.1085. The value 0.90 is P(− | no disease), the test's specificity, a different conditional probability altogether.

questions.q: Events A and B have P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4 and are mutually exclusive. Which statement is true?
options: A and B are not independent, because P(A ∩ B) = 0 while P(A)P(B) = 0.12
A and B are independent, because one cannot influence the other
questions.why: Mutually exclusive means P(A ∩ B) = 0, which differs from P(A)P(B) = 0.12, so they are dependent: learning B occurred tells you A did not. The claim that they are independent confuses 'cannot happen together' with 'carry no information about each other'. P(A ∪ B) = 0.58 uses 0.3 + 0.4 − 0.12, subtracting an intersection computed as if the events were independent; for disjoint events the union is 0.7. P(A | B) = 0.3 also assumes independence; in fact P(A | B) = 0/0.4 = 0.

questions.q: Factory A produces 60% of a firm's output, with 2% defective. Factory B produces the rest, with 5% defective. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen item is defective. (b) Given that an item is defective, find the probability it came from factory A. (c) Are 'defective' and 'from factory A' independent? Explain.
markScheme: (a) Uses the law of total probability with the partition {A, B}
(b) Bayes: P(A | defective) = 0.012/0.032 = 0.375
(c) Not independent: P(A | defective) = 0.375 ≠ P(A) = 0.6 (or P(defective | A) = 0.02 ≠ 0.032)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) The factories partition the output, so by the law of total probability P(D) = P(D | A)P(A) + P(D | B)P(B) = 0.02 × 0.6 + 0.05 × 0.4 = 0.012 + 0.02 = 0.032. (b) By Bayes' theorem, P(A | D) = P(D | A)P(A)/P(D) = 0.012/0.032 = 0.375. (c) They are not independent: P(A | D) = 0.375 differs from P(A) = 0.6. Equivalently P(D | A) = 0.02 differs from P(D) = 0.032. Learning an item is defective makes it less likely that it came from A, because A has the lower defect rate.

questions.q: X takes the values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3. What is Var(X)?
questions.why: E(X) = 1.1 and E(X²) = 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7, so Var(X) = 1.7 − 1.1² = 0.49. The value 1.7 is E(X²), with the squared mean never subtracted. The value 0.7 is the standard deviation, √0.49. The value 0.6 subtracts E(X) = 1.1 instead of [E(X)]² = 1.21.

questions.q: Var(X) = 4. What is Var(3X − 2)?
questions.why: Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X) = 9 × 4 = 36; the constant −2 shifts location and does not affect variance. The value 10 applies the transformation to the variance itself (3 × 4 − 2). The value 12 multiplies by a = 3 instead of a² = 9. The value 34 squares the multiplier correctly but then wrongly subtracts the constant (36 − 2).

questions.q: A continuous random variable X has density f(x) = cx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and 0 otherwise. (a) Find c. (b) Find the cdf F(x). (c) Find E(X) and Var(X). (d) Find the median of X.
markScheme: (a) ∫ cx dx from 0 to 1 = c/2 = 1, so c = 2
(b) F(x) = 0 for x < 0, x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 1 for x > 1
(c) E(X) = ∫ 2x² dx = 2/3; E(X²) = ∫ 2x³ dx = 1/2
questions.modelAnswer: (a) The density must integrate to 1: ∫ cx dx from 0 to 1 = c/2 = 1, so c = 2. (b) For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, F(x) = ∫ 2t dt from 0 to x = x². So F(x) = 0 for x < 0, x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and 1 for x > 1. (c) E(X) = ∫ x · 2x dx = 2/3. E(X²) = ∫ x² · 2x dx = 2/4 = 1/2. Var(X) = 1/2 − (2/3)² = 1/2 − 4/9 = 1/18 ≈ 0.0556. (d) The median m solves F(m) = 1/2, so m² = 1/2 and m = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. This is above the mean of 0.667, consistent with the density being skewed to the left (more mass near 1).

questions.q: X ~ Binomial(10, 0.3). What is P(X = 2), to 4 decimal places?
questions.why: P(X = 2) = 10C2 × 0.3² × 0.7⁸ = 45 × 0.09 × 0.0576 ≈ 0.2335. The value 0.0052 leaves out the factor 10C2 = 45, counting only one ordering of the two successes. The value 0.3828 is the cumulative P(X ≤ 2), not the single probability. The value 0.0014 swaps p and 1 − p, computing 45 × 0.7² × 0.3⁸.

questions.q: Calls arrive at a help desk as a Poisson process at an average rate of 2 per minute. What is the probability of at least 2 calls in a given minute?
questions.why: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(0) − P(1) = 1 − e^(−2)(1 + 2) ≈ 0.594. The value 0.271 is P(X = 2) only, ignoring 3 or more calls. The value 0.406 is P(X ≤ 1), the complement of the event asked for. The value 0.865 is 1 − P(0), the probability of at least one call, which forgets to remove P(X = 1).

questions.q: Using the representation of a binomial random variable as a sum of Bernoulli random variables, derive the mean and variance of X ~ Binomial(n, p). State the assumption your derivation needs.
markScheme: Writes X = X1 + … + Xn with Xi ~ Bernoulli(p)
Computes E(Xi) = p and Var(Xi) = E(Xi²) − p² = p − p² = p(1 − p)
Uses linearity of expectation: E(X) = np
Uses independence so variances add: Var(X) = np(1 − p)
States independence of trials is needed for the variance (not for the mean)
questions.modelAnswer: Let Xi = 1 if trial i is a success and 0 otherwise, so each Xi ~ Bernoulli(p) and X = X1 + X2 + … + Xn counts the successes. For one trial, E(Xi) = 1 × p + 0 × (1 − p) = p. Since Xi² = Xi, E(Xi²) = p and Var(Xi) = p − p² = p(1 − p). By linearity of expectation, which holds whether or not the Xi are independent, E(X) = ΣE(Xi) = np. Because the trials are independent, all covariances between different Xi are zero, so Var(X) = ΣVar(Xi) = np(1 − p). Independence is needed for the variance result: with dependent trials (for example sampling without replacement, giving the hypergeometric) the mean is unchanged but the variance differs.

questions.q: X ~ N(50, 16). What is P(X > 56)?
questions.why: σ = √16 = 4, so z = (56 − 50)/4 = 1.5 and P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668. The value 0.3538 standardises with the variance, z = 6/16 = 0.375, instead of the standard deviation. The value 0.9332 is Φ(1.5) = P(X < 56), the wrong tail. The value 0.1336 is the two-tailed P(|Z| > 1.5), double the one tail asked for.

questions.q: A component's lifetime is exponential with mean 2 years. Given that it has already lasted 2 years, what is the probability that it lasts at least 2 more years?
questions.why: The rate is λ = 1/2. By the memoryless property, P(X > 4 | X > 2) = P(X > 2) = e^(−0.5 × 2) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. The value e^(−2) is the unconditional P(X > 4), which ignores the information that it has survived 2 years. The value 1 − e^(−1) is the probability that it fails within the next 2 years. The value e^(−4) uses the mean 2 as if it were the rate λ, giving e^(−2 × 2).

questions.q: X ~ Binomial(100, 0.5). Use a normal approximation with continuity correction to estimate P(X ≤ 55). Explain why the approximation is reasonable and why the continuity correction is used.
markScheme: Mean np = 50 and variance np(1 − p) = 25, so SD 5
Justifies: n large and p = 0.5 gives a symmetric distribution, np and n(1 − p) both well above 5
Applies continuity correction: P(X ≤ 55) ≈ P(Y ≤ 55.5)
Explains the correction: a discrete value k corresponds to the interval (k − 0.5, k + 0.5) under the continuous approximation
questions.modelAnswer: X has mean np = 50 and variance np(1 − p) = 25, so standard deviation 5. With n = 100 and p = 0.5, np = n(1 − p) = 50, well above the usual threshold of about 5, and p = 0.5 makes the binomial symmetric, so the N(50, 25) approximation is good. The binomial puts probability on whole numbers, while the normal is continuous; treating each integer k as the interval from k − 0.5 to k + 0.5 means P(X ≤ 55) should be approximated by P(Y ≤ 55.5). Then z = (55.5 − 50)/5 = 1.1 and P(X ≤ 55) ≈ Φ(1.1) ≈ 0.864. The exact binomial probability is also about 0.864, whereas ignoring the correction gives Φ(1.0) ≈ 0.841.

questions.q: X and Y each take the values 0 or 1, with p(0,0) = 0.3, p(0,1) = 0.2, p(1,0) = 0.1 and p(1,1) = 0.4. What is Cov(X, Y)?
questions.why: E(X) = 0.5, E(Y) = 0.6 and E(XY) = P(X = 1, Y = 1) = 0.4, so Cov = 0.4 − 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.1. The value 0.4 is E(XY) without subtracting E(X)E(Y). The value 0.41 is the correlation, 0.1/√(0.25 × 0.24), not the covariance. The value 0.3 is E(X)E(Y), the term that should be subtracted.

questions.q: Var(X) = 4, Var(Y) = 9 and Cov(X, Y) = 2. What is Var(X − Y)?
questions.why: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2Cov(X, Y) = 4 + 9 − 4 = 9. The value 17 adds the covariance term, the formula for Var(X + Y). The value 13 ignores the covariance, which is only right if X and Y are uncorrelated. The value −5 subtracts the variances; a variance can never be negative, and the coefficient on Y is squared, so Var(Y) enters with a plus sign.

questions.q: Show that if X and Y are independent then Cov(X, Y) = 0, and give an example showing that the converse is false.
markScheme: Uses Cov(X, Y) = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y)
Shows E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) under independence by factorising the joint pmf/pdf in the sum or integral
Example: X uniform on {−1, 0, 1}, Y = X²
Computes E(X) = 0 and E(XY) = E(X³) = 0, so Cov = 0
Shows dependence, e.g. P(X = 0, Y = 1) = 0 ≠ P(X = 0)P(Y = 1) = (1/3)(2/3)
questions.modelAnswer: Cov(X, Y) = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y). If X and Y are independent (discrete case), p(x, y) = pX(x)pY(y), so E(XY) = ΣΣ xy pX(x)pY(y) = (Σ x pX(x))(Σ y pY(y)) = E(X)E(Y), hence Cov = 0. The continuous case is the same with integrals. The converse fails. Let X take −1, 0, 1 with probability 1/3 each and let Y = X². Then E(X) = 0 and E(XY) = E(X³) = (−1 + 0 + 1)/3 = 0, so Cov(X, Y) = 0 − 0 × E(Y) = 0. But X and Y are clearly dependent: P(X = 0, Y = 1) = 0, while P(X = 0)P(Y = 1) = (1/3)(2/3) = 2/9. Covariance only picks up linear association, and here the relationship is quadratic.

questions.q:
The joint probability mass function of X and Y is: P(X=1, Y=0) = 0.10, P(X=2, Y=0) = 0.20, P(X=3, Y=0) = 0.10, P(X=1, Y=1) = 0.20, P(X=2, Y=1) = 0.10, P(X=3, Y=1) = 0.30.
(a) Find the marginal distributions of X and Y and determine whether X and Y are independent. [4]
(b) Find E(X), Var(X), E(Y) and Var(Y). [5]
(c) Find Cov(X, Y) and Corr(X, Y). [4]
(d) Find the conditional distribution of X given Y = 1 and hence E(X | Y = 1). [4]
(e) Find Var(2X − 3Y). [3]
markScheme: (a) Not independent: e.g. P(X=1, Y=0) = 0.10 ≠ 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12

questions.q:
The time X (in hours) that a component takes to complete a task has density f(x) = kx(2 − x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and 0 otherwise.
(a) Show that k = 3/4. [3]
(b) Find the cdf of X and show that the median is 1. [4]
(c) Find E(X) and Var(X). [5]
(d) Show that P(X > 1.5) = 5/32. [3]
(e) Ten components work independently. Find the probability that at least one of them takes more than 1.5 hours, and the expected number that do. [5]
markScheme: (b) F(x) = (3/4)(x² − x³/3) on [0, 2], 0 below and 1 above
(b) F(1) = (3/4)(2/3) = 1/2, so the median is 1 (also by symmetry about 1)
(c) E(X) = 1 (symmetry or integration); E(X²) = (3/4)(8 − 32/5) = 6/5
(e) Number exceeding 1.5 hours ~ Bin(10, 5/32); P(at least one) = 1 − (27/32)¹⁰ ≈ 0.817
(e) Expected number = 10 × 5/32 = 1.5625
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The density must integrate to 1. ∫ x(2 − x) dx from 0 to 2 = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4 − 8/3 = 4/3. So k × 4/3 = 1 and k = 3/4. Also kx(2 − x) ≥ 0 on [0, 2], so f is a valid density.

(b) For 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, F(x) = (3/4)∫ t(2 − t) dt from 0 to x = (3/4)(x² − x³/3). F(x) = 0 for x < 0 and 1 for x > 2. Check F(2) = (3/4)(4 − 8/3) = 1. F(1) = (3/4)(1 − 1/3) = (3/4)(2/3) = 1/2, so the median is 1. This is also clear because f is symmetric about x = 1 (f(1 + u) = f(1 − u)).

(c) By symmetry about 1, E(X) = 1. Checking: E(X) = (3/4)∫(2x² − x³)dx = (3/4)(16/3 − 4) = (3/4)(4/3) = 1. E(X²) = (3/4)∫(2x³ − x⁴)dx from 0 to 2 = (3/4)(8 − 32/5) = (3/4)(8/5) = 6/5. Var(X) = 6/5 − 1² = 1/5 = 0.2, so the SD is about 0.447 hours.

(d) P(X > 1.5) = 1 − F(1.5) = 1 − (3/4)(2.25 − 3.375/3) = 1 − (3/4)(2.25 − 1.125) = 1 − (3/4)(1.125) = 1 − 0.84375 = 0.15625 = 5/32.

(e) Let N be the number of the ten components taking more than 1.5 hours. With independent components each exceeding 1.5 hours with probability 5/32, N ~ Binomial(10, 5/32). P(N ≥ 1) = 1 − P(N = 0) = 1 − (27/32)¹⁰ ≈ 1 − 0.183 = 0.817. E(N) = 10 × 5/32 = 1.5625.
